Valid Parentheses
O(n) / O(n). Use ArrayDeque, not the legacy Stack class.
Isomorphic Strings ("egg" ↔ "add")

The mapping must be one-to-one in both directions, so a single map is not enough ("badc" vs "baba"). Recording the last index for each character in both strings checks both directions at once. O(n) time, O(1) space. "Word Pattern" is the same problem with words instead of characters.
Valid Palindrome II (at most one deletion)
On the first mismatch you only need to try deleting the left or the right character once. O(n) time, O(1) space.
Palindromic Substrings: count them all
Same expand-around-centre idea as Longest Palindromic Substring, but count every successful expansion. O(n²) time, O(1) space. Manacher's algorithm does it in O(n), but is rarely expected.
String to Integer (atoi) with overflow handling
The key interview point is detecting overflow before it happens: check res > (MAX - d) / 10 instead of multiplying first. Clamping to MIN_VALUE for negatives works because |MIN| = MAX + 1. O(n) time.
Roman to Integer

A symbol smaller than the one after it is subtracted, otherwise added. O(n). The reverse (Integer to Roman) is greedy: walk a table of values 1000, 900, 500, 400 ... 1 and append each symbol while it fits.
Encode and Decode a List of Strings

Any delimiter alone can appear inside a string, so prefix each string with its length. The decoder reads the length and jumps exactly that far, so # inside the data is harmless. O(total length). This is the same idea as length-prefixed framing in network protocols.
Find a pattern in a text: KMP (strStr)

The naive approach (or String.indexOf) is O(n·m) in the worst case. KMP precomputes the LPS table so that after a mismatch the pattern shifts without re-reading text characters: O(n + m) time, O(m) space. Mention Rabin-Karp (rolling hash) as the alternative for multiple patterns.
String += in a loop vs StringBuilder vs String.join

| s += x in a loop | StringBuilder | String.join / Collectors.joining
Cost for n appends | O(n²) characters copied (new String each time) | O(n) amortized | O(n)
Mutable | No | Yes (also reverse, insert, setCharAt) | No
Thread-safe | Immutable, so yes | No (StringBuffer is, but slower) | Yes
Best for | A few fixed concatenations | Building output char by char | Joining a list with a separator
Rule of thumb: any concatenation inside a loop should use a StringBuilder. The compiler only optimises single expressions like a + b + c, not loops.
Anagram check: int[26] vs HashMap vs sorting

| int[26] counts | HashMap<Character,Integer> | Sort both strings
Time | O(n) | O(n) average | O(n log n)
Extra space | O(1) (26 ints) | O(k) distinct chars | O(n) for the char arrays
Character set | Lowercase a-z only | Any (Unicode) | Any
As a group key (Group Anagrams) | Arrays.toString(count) | Awkward | new String(sortedChars)
Rule of thumb: lowercase letters only → int[26]. Unicode or "any characters" → HashMap. Sorting is the shortest code and fine when the strings are short.
Longest Palindromic Substring: expand around centre vs DP table vs Manacher

| Expand around centre | DP table | Manacher
Time | O(n²) | O(n²) | O(n)
Extra space | O(1) | O(n²) booleans | O(n)
Idea | Grow from each of 2n - 1 centres | dp[i][j] = s[i]==s[j] && dp[i+1][j-1] | Reuse mirror radii inside the rightmost palindrome
Interview fit | Best: short and clear | Good if you want to show DP | Rarely expected; mention only
Interview tip: code expand-around-centre. Mention that the DP table gives the same time with more memory, and that Manacher exists for O(n).
Substring search: indexOf vs KMP vs Rabin-Karp

| Naive / String.indexOf | KMP | Rabin-Karp
Worst case | O(n · m) | O(n + m) | O(n · m) on many hash collisions
Typical case | Fast in practice | O(n + m) | O(n + m) expected
Extra space | O(1) | O(m) prefix (LPS) table | O(1)
Strength | Simple, built in | Guaranteed linear, never moves back in the text | Many patterns of the same length; rolling hash reuse
Rule of thumb: in real code use indexOf. In an interview that asks for a guaranteed linear bound, use KMP. Use a rolling hash when comparing many equal-length windows (for example, repeated DNA sequences).
